va_pinball_wall.blurb: A short boulder wall in the Nature Loop section of Grayson County Recreation Park, in southwest Virginia. It is the first big boulder you meet when walking the trail, with a smaller block tucked directly beneath it. Sixteen problems, most between V1 and V4, with two V5s at the top end. Many of the lines are overhanging and covered in big holds, and they are low enough that one or two pads should be plenty. The main drawback is that the tops are grubby, and some people finish by way of a tree. A handy warm-up spot or a friendly stop for newer boulderers.

va_led_zeppelin_boulders.blurb: A small cluster of boulders beside the Potomac Heritage Trail, just upstream of Windy Run Park in northern Virginia and close to Washington DC. Sixteen problems that lean easy: about eleven are V0 or V1, a couple sit around V2 and V3, and a few much harder lines go up to V6. The rock is decent for the easier problems and notably good on the hard ones. Because it is right on a busy riverside path, expect walkers passing by and keep the group small. A short hike from the car makes it a fine after-work session.
va_led_zeppelin_boulders.parking_note: Leave the car in the Windy Run Park lot, then walk down toward the Potomac River.
va_led_zeppelin_boulders.approach: From the Windy Run Park lot, hike down to the Potomac and take the steps beside the waterfall. Turn left and follow the river upstream; the boulder cluster is on your left.

wa_shangri_la.blurb: A secluded crag in the Far Side zone of the Exit 38 area off I-90, near North Bend. It sits on a forested buttress across a big talus field, with cairns marking the way. Sixteen routes: mostly bolted sport lines of 50 to 100 feet, plus a few trad leads. The grades centre on 5.10 and 5.11, with several 5.12s and a couple of easier 5.7 and 5.8 lines. The rock is clean and grippy, the bolts are spaced further apart than at neighbouring crags, and the numbers feel closer to Index than to the rest of Exit 38. It dries quickly after rain and has views toward the high country.

wa_lower_wall_3.blurb: The smaller of the cliffs that make up the Western Front on Burge Mountain, outside Tonasket in the Okanogan. Sixteen routes of roughly 50 to 75 feet, mostly bolted sport with a few trad lines. The grades are approachable: the bulk run from 5.7 through 5.10, with a few 5.11s at the top end. It is a short walk from the parking area, and the wider Western Front area is partly shaded and mostly quiet, with the occasional local around. A good choice for a relaxed day of moderate single-pitch climbing.

wa_north_fork_cliff.blurb: A remote, lightly developed trad wall above the North Fork of the Tieton River in south-central Washington. About sixteen routes, mostly long single-pitch or two-pitch lines near 160 feet, on grippy andesite that climbs somewhat like granite. Grades run from 5.8 to 5.11, with most at 5.10 and 5.11. The wall faces north, so it works on hot summer days, with sun arriving mid to late afternoon. The season is short: snow can linger at the base into June and it turns chilly by mid-September. Expect solitude, a long steep walk in and out, and views over the surrounding lakes and wilderness.

wa_shadow_wall.blurb: A shaded sport wall on the lower part of the main face at Calendar Butte, near Walker Valley in northwest Washington. Sixteen routes, nearly all bolted with a single trad line, spanning 5.10 to 5.12 in roughly even thirds. That makes it a place for climbers already leading in the 5.10s and up. Tall trees shade the base and the shorter routes on the right, so it is a favourite when the weather is hot. The butte's full wall reaches about 160 feet, so bring a long rope, and new routes are still being added.

wa_wankers_columns.blurb: A short crag of columns in the Columbia Gorge on the Washington side, climbed on gear or on top rope. Sixteen routes, about nine trad and seven top-rope, mostly 30 to 50 feet tall. The climbing is sustained and crack-based, with stiff thin finger cracks and a few hand cracks. Grades run from 5.6 to 5.12, centred on 5.10 and 5.11, with a few easier leads in the 5.7 range. Anchors at the top let you lead or set a rope. The columns stay dry much of the time and get hot in summer, so this is mainly a winter option. Poison oak grows at the base.
